speaker: N
text: In 1956, a man grabbed the wrong part from a box, and his machine started beating like a heart.

speaker: N
text: His name was Wilson Greatbatch, and he was building a gadget to record heartbeats.

speaker: N
text: He reached for a tiny resistor.

speaker: N
text: But he grabbed one a hundred times too strong.

speaker: N
text: He soldered it in, switched it on, and froze.

speaker: N
text: The circuit went quiet, then pulsed.

speaker: N
text: Quiet, pulse.

speaker: N
text: Quiet, pulse.

speaker: N
text: Once every second, just like a heart.

speaker: N
text: Meanwhile, doctors had patients whose hearts kept slowing down until they stopped.

speaker: N
text: The only machines that could help were as big as a TV and plugged into the wall.

speaker: N
text: If the power went out, the patient was in serious trouble.

speaker: N
text: You see, every heartbeat starts with a tiny electrical spark.

speaker: N
text: In those patients, the spark wasn't getting through.

speaker: N
text: And Wilson's mistake made the exact spark a heart needs, once every second.

speaker: N
text: So he shrank it until it fit in the palm of your hand.

speaker: N
text: He quit his job and built them in the barn behind his house.

speaker: N
text: In 1960, surgeons placed one inside a seventy-seven-year-old man.

speaker: N
text: His heart beat steady again.

speaker: N
text: Today, millions of people walk around with one in their chest.

speaker: N
text: All because of one wrong part from one box.

speaker: N
text: And it all began when...
